### Stations Is the Book of the Week, Godzilla Is Back Bigger, and the Night Shift Is Hell

Filed as: Sunday Review of Reviews — Weekend Features · 2026-11-08T04:10:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-08-sunday-reviews.html

Weekend Features — Sunday Review of Reviews

 Objective

 Stations Is the Book of the Week, Godzilla Is Back Bigger, and the Night Shift Is Hell

 The week's review lists were tallied, and the tally was not close. The book du jour is Stations by Louise Kennedy, published in the United States on November 3: first in the week's fiction tally with nine rave reviews and no mixed or negative verdict filed against it, taken by its reviewers to be a love story about two Irish teenagers whose bond runs 25 years through exile, addiction and London. On screen the week belonged to work: Dead-End Job, the Korean serial on Netflix in which a man in debt takes night jobs at 50 times the wage and finds a monster on every shift, drew 5.0 million views in three days; and Godzilla Minus Zero opened in cinemas to complete agreement on its effects and open disagreement on whether bigger is better. The desk states its position plainly at the head of each part: it has not read the book, and it has not watched the serial or the films. What follows is a review of reviews.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0410 ET, Sunday, November 8, 2026. The first Sunday Review of Reviews of this paper, filed under the Weekend Features ruling of November 4, 2026. The desk tallied the week's review lists—the New York Times Book Review and its peers, the Chicago Review of Books, the Washington reviewing tradition carried in Ron Charles's Tuesday Review, the Guardian, the Boston Globe, and the aggregating tally at Book Marks—and the week's film and television reviews, international by house rule. The clippings the report was drawn from are filed beneath it, each stamped subjective.

The Week in Brief: The Tally

In fiction, one book stood clear of the field, and the field itself was strong. Book Marks' tally of the week, published November 6, ranks Stations first with nine rave reviews and no other verdict recorded. Behind it: Tom Drury's West of Loveland, five rave and one positive, its New York Times review by Daniel Mason among the week's five selected reviews; Ian Rankin's The Heights, three rave, three positive and one mixed, the week's one divided verdict among the leaders; Kit de Waal's Sweet Pea, four rave and one positive; and Lucy Apps's Gloria Don't Speak, two rave and one positive. In nonfiction the lead was split: D. J. Taylor's The King Under the Mountain, a book in search of J. R. R. Tolkien, carried five rave, one positive and three mixed—the most argued-over book on either list. Judi Dench's memoir Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? carried five rave and no dissent; Dan Jones's Castles four rave and one positive, its New York Times Book Review notice among them; Simon Garfield's The Pen three rave and two positive; and Mark Binelli's life of Martin Scorsese in film, Just a Shot Away, four rave. The week's five selected single reviews, chosen November 5, were Dwight Garner in the Times on Annie Proulx's Stories, Clare Clark in the Guardian on Stations, John Semly in The Nation on William Gass's The Tunnel, Daniel Mason in the Times on Drury, and Nick Holdstock in the Guardian on William T. Vollmann's A Table for Fortune. Stations is the only title that stands at the head of the tally and inside the selected five at once. The desk takes it as the book du jour on that record.

Part One — The Book: Stations, by Louise Kennedy

The desk has not read this book. It says so plainly, as the house rule requires: everything in this part is what the reviewers report, agree on, and dispute, and nothing in it is the desk's reading. Stations is a novel. Louise Kennedy is an Irish writer who worked as a chef for almost thirty years before publishing; her first novel, Trespasses, was published in 2022 when she was 55 and was shortlisted for the Women's Prize for Fiction. Stations was published in Europe in September and in the United States by Riverhead Books on November 3, 2026: 288 pages, $28, ISBN 9780593714607. It stands on the November 2026 Indie Next List.

On what the book is, the reviewers agree completely, and their agreement is the week's firmest fact. In 1980s Ireland, R&oacute;is&iacute;n McCaffrey and Red Camelin bond as precocious, disaffected teenagers. Her father, a Catholic who had joined the Royal Ulster Constabulary, has abandoned the family after a breakdown; his father banishes him from home. The two meet again as exiles in London, where Red is squatting in an abandoned flat with no electricity among Irish exiles, gripped by addiction. The novel traces their relationship over the next 25 years, into the early 2000s: her community college and fledgling career as a writer, a marriage to an upper-class Englishman, a divorce, a return to Ireland, and a promise made to Red's ailing mother to find him and tell him it is safe to come home. Every reviewer in the file describes the same construction: dated moments, clustered, broken by silent gaps—in Ron Charles's account, one gap as long as 18 years. Every reviewer names the same ground under the story: the Troubles, Thatcher's England, the AIDS crisis, poverty, violence, addiction, shame and loss.

On what the book is taken to be, the reviewers also agree, in their own words, filed below. The Guardian's Clare Clark, in the review the week's selectors chose, takes it as a love story at its heart—furious, tender, a paean to loyalty and generosity of spirit—and at the same time an elegy to a generation of lost Irish boys, a testament to violence and fear passed from father to son. Its title, in her reading, holds two journeys at once: the transience of the diaspora, its trains and boats and coaches, and the Stations of the Cross. The Boston Globe's verdict, carried in the tally, calls the book extraordinary and bittersweet, finds a lived-in circumspection in Kennedy's work, and places her alongside Eimear McBride and Sally Rooney. People calls it a marvel. Joumana Khatib of the New York Times, in the praise filed with the book, states that she loved it and highly recommends it. Charles takes it as a story of devotion, addiction and the limits of friendship, and asks the question he puts at the centre of his review: what does a person owe a brilliant best friend who pushes her away while grasping for her, and how much of her impatience rests on ignorance of what happened to him.

The split in the file is narrow, and it is about the ending and the weight, not about the writing. The Chicago Review of Books, in Eileen Zampa's review, is the fullest statement of the reservation: Kennedy creates a satisfying tension between a modern reader's sensibilities and R&oacute;is&iacute;n's painstaking evolution, deftly draws out her shame, denial and avoidance, and refuses to wrap her life in a neat bow; the final pages leave her future unresolved and the reader with questions, and some readers may find the ending frustrating. Clark's Guardian review reaches the same place from the other side: the novel is too subtle and clear-eyed to offer easy answers to whether cycles of anguish or neglect can be broken, or whether love in all its frustrating insufficiency is enough to save anyone—and its unanswered questions are the point, the thing that burns. Charles records extravagant grief carried in the prose, and a book that is hard to close because desire and melancholy pull on opposite sides of it. No reviewer in the week's file faults the sentences. The disagreement is whether an unresolved life, left unresolved on the page, is a frustration or a fidelity. The desk files the disagreement as it stands: it is the only one the week produced about this book.

The record around the book is part of its reception, and the reviewers file it the same way. Publishers Weekly's profile establishes that Kennedy took her characters' road herself: she moved to London in the 1980s under an offer of four weeks of unemployment benefits to anyone who agreed to leave Ireland for five years, and Clark credits that history for a 1980s London evoked with almost hallucinogenic precision—squats, gas heaters, and not enough change for the payphone. The profile also records that she began the book at a breakneck pace after a melanoma diagnosis in 2019, and that Trespasses has sold 40,000 print copies in the United States. The book the reviewers describe is therefore received, on all sides, as a second novel that confirms a late and unlikely career: a chef who decided writing was something magical people did, publishing at 55, and now placed by the Boston Globe in the company of the contemporary Irish writers whose next project its reviewer will race to read.

Where to get it. Stations by Louise Kennedy is available at Amazon. As an Amazon Associate, Objective Daily News earns from qualifying purchases made through that link.

Part Two — Screen: The Night Shift, and the Monsters

The desk has not watched any of the screen works in this part. It has not streamed Dead-End Job, and it has not sat in a cinema for Godzilla Minus Zero or Wild Horse Nine. Their status here is the same as the book's: the reviews, reviewed.

The television pick of the week is Dead-End Job, and it is Korean, and its subject is work. The series was released on Netflix on October 30, in eight episodes. Byeon Hyeok-jun, played by Lee Jae-wook, owes a loan shark over 140 million won, borrowed to repair an unwise investment by his mother. A staffing agency called Spider offers him night work at 50 times the minimum wage—4 million won for one shift, in Decider's account—under one rule, in the Korean reports: never speak about what happens at work. What happens at work is a convenience store with rules posted for midnight, a swarm of rats that clumps into a giant rat, moths, a milk delivery route, a movie theatre, an unidentified clown. Go Min-si plays an investigator looking into the agency; Kim Min-ha plays his younger sister Ji-yoon, who also takes one of the jobs; Lee Hee-jun plays the agency's manager. Netflix's own figures, reported by Sports Chosun, give the measure of its week: 25.4 million viewing hours and 5.0 million views in its first three days, No. 4 on the Global Top 10 Non-English Shows chart, No. 1 on the daily chart in Korea, and Top 10 lists in 51 countries. On FlixPatrol's separate count it reached No. 2 globally and No. 1 in 14 countries. It is, on the comparison filed by Fiction Horizon, the second-best Friday debut for a Korean binge release in 2026.

The reviewers agree on the machine, and on the performance at its centre. Decider's Joel Keller names the form first: a horror anthology whose main characters stay the same from episode to episode, in the line of Creepshow and Tales From the Crypt, each episode a new job that pays amazingly well and can be violent and horrific. His verdict is Stream It, and his performance worth watching goes not to an actor but to the effects department, for moths made creepy and a rat monster that genuinely frightened him. India Today's praise, carried in the Korean reports, goes to Lee Jae-wook: a joy to watch, capturing fear and bewilderment, oscillating between comedy and genuine dread, with Kim Min-ha comfortable in her role. The Korean and overseas reports agree on the premise's name for itself: work-to-survive horror, the everyday struggle to pay the bills paired with scares, and on IMDb, at 7.2 of 10 from over 1,500 ratings, one viewer's formulation is repeated across the file—the supernatural horror is the surface; the real terror is the debt, and the desperation that drives a man to take the job anyway.

The split is about the back half, and it is the same split the book produced, in a coarser grain. On Reddit, in the reports filed below, episode 2, the clown episode, is named the peak, with decline after it; the ending is called vague, and in India Today's cooler line, rushed; the computer graphics are said to fluctuate wildly from episode to episode; and one IMDb review gives one star on the ground that the plot makes no sense. The fullest statement of the reservation is the long viewer review on MyDramaList: an imitation of The Twilight Zone and Tales from the Crypt without the depth of the first or the dark humour of the second, enjoyable and easily forgettable, its first four episodes more polished than its last three, its episodes too short for character development, and its commentary on precarious gig work left unexploited. Decider concedes the same point in one clause—the viewer does not get to know the characters all that well—and streams it anyway. Against the reservations stands the behaviour the reports record: viewers who turned the series on at the top of the service and watched to 2 a.m., and the most common word in the finale thread, which is Season 2. Netflix has announced no second season. The desk files both records: the critics' reservation, and the audience's request.

In cinemas, the week's film is Godzilla Minus Zero, and its reviewers agree on exactly one thing. The film opened November 6, a sequel to Godzilla Minus One set in 1949, two years on, with the Shikishima family again at its centre and a second enormous creature to face. The first-reviews file and the weekend roundups agree, without exception in the clippings below, on the effects: they top the Oscar-winning work of the predecessor, the monster fights are the most majestic computer-generated action put to film in one critic's phrase, and the Academy Award for the craft is treated by more than one reviewer as a formality. Everything after that is contested. One camp holds the film even better than Minus One in every way, easily one of the best films of the year. The other camp, stated by TheWrap and repeated in the roundup of November 7, holds that it is a great Godzilla sequel, maybe one of the best, but not one of the great Godzilla movies: bigger, louder and sillier, less focused, its human elements less cohesive, and its title character off screen for long stretches, which is also the most common complaint in the whole file. Audiences, on the one measure that is not a review, sided with the first camp in the opening days: an A CinemaScore and a 96 percent audience score from over 1,000 verified ratings, in the November 7 roundup. The desk has not seen the film; it files the split as the week's honest position on it—the craft is settled, the film is not.

The week's second film is filed in one paragraph, because its reviewers agree almost as completely and argue about almost as little. Wild Horse Nine, Martin McDonagh's first film since The Banshees of Inisherin, opened November 6: John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell play CIA officers sent from Santiago to Easter Island on the eve of the 1973 coup in Chile, with Steve Buscemi as their station chief. Malkovich won the Best Actor award at Venice, and the reviews filed below credit some of the best acting of his career and of Rockwell's and Buscemi's beside him, with one quotable line after another. The reservation, where it appears, is familiarity: the film reads to its cooler reviewers as a retread of In Bruges in a sparser landscape, and its detractors are not expected to find anything new in it. Its scores in the weekend guides stand in the low-to-mid nineties. Between the two films the week therefore offers one settled craft verdict with an unsettled film attached, and one settled performance verdict with a question of novelty attached. That is the screen file, whole.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, the monster's score: Godzilla Minus Zero stands at 93 percent from 56 reviews in one weekend guide, 91 percent from 131 reviews in a second, and 90 percent from 162 reviews in the roundup updated November 7—three different counts taken at three different hours as the review file grew, printed here as a moving measure, not a contradiction the desk can resolve. Wild Horse Nine likewise stands at 93 percent from 120 reviews and 95 percent from 166 in two guides published the same weekend. Second, the Korean serial's makers: Decider credits Han Jun-hee as creator, the Sports Chosun report credits Kim Da-min as director, and Star News reports the series as co-directed by Han Jun-hee and Kim Da-min and written by Gyeong Min-sun; the desk prints all three attributions as filed and adopts none. Third, the book's tally: nine rave is Book Marks' count of the reviews it tracked for the week of November 6, and the desk's statement that no mixed or negative verdict was filed is a statement about that tally and the reviews in the clippings below, not about every review that may exist. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts are single-valued: Stations was published in the United States on November 3, 2026, by Riverhead, at 288 pages and $28, and stands first in the week's fiction tally; Dead-End Job was released on Netflix on October 30 in eight episodes and drew 25.4 million hours and 5.0 million views in three days on Netflix's own count; Godzilla Minus Zero and Wild Horse Nine both opened on November 6. The desk has not read the book and has not watched the screen works. The log proceeds to Sunday's watches.

 The Clippings Filed With This Feature

 Everything the desk read for the feature above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk's feature is the only item in this file stamped objective. Sixteen items.

 
 SubjectiveBook Marks — the best reviewed books of the week, November 6, 2026Book Marks tallies the week's reviews and ranks Louise Kennedy's Stations first in fiction with nine rave reviews and no mixed or negative verdict; Tom Drury's West of Loveland follows with five rave and one positive, Ian Rankin's The Heights with three rave, three positive and one mixed, Kit de Waal's Sweet Pea with four rave and one positive, and Lucy Apps's Gloria Don't Speak with two rave and one positive. In nonfiction, D. J. Taylor's The King Under the Mountain leads with five rave, one positive and three mixed; Judi Dench's Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? carries five rave; Dan Jones's Castles four rave and one positive; Simon Garfield's The Pen three rave and two positive; and Mark Binelli's Just a Shot Away, on Martin Scorsese, four rave. The Boston Globe's verdict on Stations, quoted in the tally, calls it extraordinary and bittersweet and places Kennedy alongside Eimear McBride and Sally Rooney.

 SubjectiveBook Marks — five reviews you need to read this week, November 5, 2026Book Marks selects five reviews of the week: Dwight Garner in The New York Times on Annie Proulx's Stories: New & Selected, Clare Clark in The Guardian on Louise Kennedy's Stations, John Semly in The Nation on William Gass's The Tunnel, Daniel Mason in The New York Times on Tom Drury's West of Loveland, and Nick Holdstock in The Guardian on William T. Vollmann's A Table for Fortune. The Stations excerpt carries Clark's account in full: a relationship traced over 25 years in dated entries broken by long gaps, a London of squats and gas heaters, an Irish diaspora scarred by poverty, violence, addiction, shame and loss, and a novel that is at its heart a love story and an elegy to a generation of lost Irish boys, its title holding both the transience of travel and the Stations of the Cross.

 SubjectiveChicago Review of Books — a haunting first love, loss and life in exile: StationsEileen Zampa reviews Stations on its American publication: since its European publication in September the novel has received critical acclaim in Ireland and England, and fans of Trespasses will not be disappointed. Róisín and Redmond are two outsiders navigating family trauma, addiction and exile in Ireland and London from the 1980s to the early 2000s; Kennedy creates a tension between a modern reader's sensibilities and Róisín's character evolution, refuses to wrap her life in a neat bow, and leaves her future unresolved in the final pages, which some readers may find frustrating. The review calls the novel sweeping in thematic scope, with deft prose and unforgettable characters, in the tradition of Irish literature from Edna O'Brien to Claire Keegan.

 SubjectiveRon Charles, The Tuesday Review — the demands of love: StationsRon Charles reviews Stations as a story of devotion, addiction and the limits of friendship: Róisín McCaffrey and Red Camelin meet as teenagers, and neither recovers from the moment of happiness. Kennedy constructs the novel as a series of dated moments over a quarter century, with silent gaps of days and one of 18 years; her prose mixes narration and internal reflection, and her dialogue, without quotation marks, captures the erratic structure of real conversation. Charles records that Kennedy worked as a chef for decades before publishing, that Trespasses, published in 2022 when she was 55, was shortlisted for the Women's Prize for Fiction, and that with Stations she has confirmed her status as a writer whose stories compete with the reader's own life. The book is listed at 288 pages and $28 from Riverhead Books.

 SubjectiveWatermark Books — Stations, the publisher's record and the praise filed with itThe bookseller's page for Stations lists Riverhead Books, publication November 3, 2026, 288 pages, ISBN 9780593714607, and the November 2026 Indie Next List. The praise carried on the page includes People calling the book a marvel, The Guardian calling it blisteringly good with questions that burn themselves into the reader's heart, Joumana Khatib of the New York Times stating she loved the book and highly recommends it, the Boston Globe on Kennedy writing about love like Sappho, and the Chicago Review of Books on its sweeping scope. The page's description states the novel's ground: in 1980s Ireland, Róisín and Red bond as precocious and disaffected teenagers, and the past hovers over the present with terrible and sometimes redemptive power.

 SubjectivePublishers Weekly — Louise Kennedy has found her homePublishers Weekly profiles Kennedy ahead of Stations: as a young woman she followed the same migratory path as her characters, moving to London in the 1980s after accepting an offer of four weeks of unemployment benefits to anyone who agreed to leave Ireland for five years. The novel is shot through with the political and social issues of Thatcher's England, including the Troubles and the AIDS crisis, and is focused primarily on the characters: Róisín McCaffrey and Red Camelin, on the dole in a decrepit London squat. The profile records her melanoma diagnosis in 2019, the breakneck approach she took to the first chapters, and that Trespasses has sold 40,000 print copies in the United States to date by BookScan's count.

 SubjectiveDecider — stream it or skip it: Dead-End Job on NetflixJoel Keller reviews the Korean series Dead-End Job: Byeon Hyeok-jun, played by Lee Jae-wook, owes a violent loan shark over 140 million won after an unwise investment by his mother, and takes night work from the Spider Staffing Agency at 50 times minimum wage. The series works as a horror anthology whose main characters stay the same, in the line of Creepshow and Tales From the Crypt; the effects department is named the performance worth watching, for moths made creepy and a rat monster formed from hundreds of rats. The verdict is Stream It: a fun ride for horror fans, even if the viewer does not get to know the characters all that well.

 SubjectiveStar News, K-EYES — Dead-End Job earns praise from overseas viewers, No. 2 globallyStar News reports the overseas reception of Dead-End Job, released October 30: an eight-part mystery horror fantasy about Byun Hyuk-jun, pursued by over 140 million won in loan-shark debt, sent by a suspicious staffing agency to workplaces including convenience stores, milk delivery routes and movie theatres. On FlixPatrol's count the series reached No. 2 on Netflix's global ranking after November 1 and No. 1 in 14 countries; on IMDb it holds 7.2 of 10 from over 1,500 ratings. Decider's Stream It verdict and India Today's praise of Lee Jae-wook are recorded, as are the Reddit splits: episode 2 named the peak with decline after it, the ending called vague, and the computer graphics said to fluctuate from episode to episode, beside the most common word in the finale thread, Season 2.

 SubjectiveSports Chosun — Dead-End Job debuts at No. 4 on the Global Top 10 Non-English Shows chartSports Chosun reports Netflix's own Top 10 figures for Dead-End Job: 25.4 million viewing hours and 5 million views in the three days after its October 30 release, fourth on the Global Top 10 Non-English Shows chart, first on the daily Top 10 in Korea, and on Top 10 lists in 51 countries including Brazil, Egypt, France, Germany, Hong Kong, India, Italy, Malaysia, Mexico, the Philippines, Saudi Arabia and Thailand. The series is described as work-to-survive horror: a young person takes a part-time job through a strange staffing agency advertising plum gigs at 50 times the usual hourly wage and is sent to nightmarish workplaces. Lee Jae-wook, Go Min-si, Kim Min-ha and Lee Hee-jun star.

 SubjectiveFiction Horizon — Dead-End Job lands one of Netflix's strongest K-drama debuts of the yearFiction Horizon places the Dead-End Job debut in the year's Korean field: 5.0 million views and 25.4 million hours between October 26 and November 1, No. 4 on the Non-English TV chart, and the second-best Friday debut for a Korean binge release in 2026, behind Teach You a Lesson at 6.4 million views and ahead of The East Palace at 4.9 million, Can This Love Be Translated? at 4 million and Our Sticky Love at 3.2 million. The eight-episode series, originally known as Perfect Job, premiered October 30; because it launched on a Friday, its debut week captured only a few days of viewing, and its second week will show whether it has staying power.

 SubjectiveMyDramaList — a viewer review of Dead-End JobA long viewer review on MyDramaList gives the cooler account: the series is an imitation of The Twilight Zone and Tales from the Crypt without the psychological and societal depth of the first or the dark humour of the second, enjoyable for a popcorn evening and easily forgettable, and not the horror series of the year. The episodic format works at first and the atmosphere succeeds, with neat direction, successful special effects and a perfect lead performance; the episodes after the first four are less inspired, the episodes are too short for character development and world-building, the commentary on precarious gig work is not exploited to its full potential, and the last three episodes are much less convincing.

 SubjectiveRotten Tomatoes Editorial — Godzilla Minus Zero, first reviewsRotten Tomatoes collects the first reviews of Godzilla Minus Zero after its New York Film Festival premiere, ahead of its November 6 opening: a sequel to Godzilla Minus One set two years later, following the Shikishima family as the monster returns to face another enormous creature. The collected verdicts agree the film is bigger and more surprising, with visual effects that top the predecessor's Oscar-winning work; they disagree on whether it is better than the previous film, one critic calling it even better in every way and another recording that with great expectations come considerable letdowns, that it lacks the clarity of purpose of Minus One, and that the human elements are not as cohesive.

 Subjective9to5Marvel — Godzilla Minus Zero reviews: 90 percent, an A CinemaScoreA reviews roundup updated November 7 records Godzilla Minus Zero at 90 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 162 reviews, with an A CinemaScore and a 96 percent audience score from over 1,000 verified ratings. Critics praise the visual effects, the IMAX-scale monster fights and the direction; the most common complaint is that the film is less focused than Godzilla Minus One and keeps Godzilla off screen for long stretches, and plenty of the same critics call it bigger, louder and sillier than Minus One, not better. GamesRadar+ is quoted calling it easily one of the best films of the year; TheWrap's cooler verdict is that it is a great Godzilla sequel, maybe one of the best, but not one of the great Godzilla movies. The film is set in 1949 and follows the Shikishima family again.

 SubjectiveSneeze Gang — new movies this weekend: Godzilla, the Cat, and Malkovich on Easter IslandA weekend roundup of the November 6 releases: Godzilla Minus Zero is expected to finish first at the box office, with forecasts from $24 million to $35 million and Variety at about $30 million, critics at 91 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 131 reviews, and the argument stated as whether it is better than Minus One, the effects agreed and the rest still fought over. The review credits some of the best acting ever done by Malkovich, Rockwell and Steve Buscemi, a fragmented supporting turn by Parker Posey, and one quotable line after another.

### The Three at Home Are Named in Kraków, a Mandate Is Given in Jerusalem, and Two Tankers Burn Without Names

Filed as: Edition No. 19 — The Overnight Watch · 2026-11-08T04:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-08-overnight-watch.html

The Night File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 The Three at Home Are Named in Kraków, a Mandate Is Given in Jerusalem, and Two Tankers Burn Without Names

 The night file, while Washington slept: Poland entered its mourning at midnight with the Kraków case completed in its outline — the three found dead at the suspect’s home identified as his parents and his sister, the suspect himself named by the prosecutors’ spokesman, and no motive established. Jerusalem supplied the night’s one new mandate: the president chose the opposition leader over the sitting prime minister to try first at a government. In the Gulf of Oman an Emirati crew pulled 22 men off a burning ship that no authority has named, in the same waters where two tankers are reported burning without names of their own. The count in Mississippi and Alaska did not move. Sunday opens as a day of mourning in Poland and the main day of Diwali in India, with the markets closed and the week’s questions — Hormuz, Abu Dhabi, the count — all waiting on Tuesday.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Sunday, November 8, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 18, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, which filed the detention order in Asunción, the three bodies at the Kraków suspect’s home, and the first tanker reports. The reports filed here are the night’s reports, taken after that edition closed; where they restate Saturday’s facts, the restatement is identified. The midnight edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

The Night in Brief

The night named three dead, handed out one mandate, and rescued 22 men from a ship it did not name. In Poland, the mourning declared for Sunday and Monday began at midnight, and Sunday morning brought the identification the Midnight Watch left as a strong indication: the three people found dead at the Kraków suspect’s home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski are his parents and his 21-year-old sister, the police confirmed. The prosecutors’ spokesman confirmed the detained man is Michał O., 24. No charge has been announced and no motive has been established. In Jerusalem, President Isaac Herzog informed Gadi Eisenkot on Saturday evening that he will be tasked with forming Israel’s next government, after factions representing 67 lawmakers recommended him against 46 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu; the formal handover is set for Sunday afternoon, and Mr. Eisenkot will have 28 days. In the waters east of the Strait of Hormuz, the United Arab Emirates National Guard rescued all 22 crew of a cargo ship on fire in the Gulf of Oman, every man stable, the ship unnamed and the fire’s cause unstated — while Iran’s Revolutionary Guards issued the full text of their tanker statement: two tankers, one in the strait’s eastern part and one within it, burning after striking mines on unauthorized routes with their navigation and positioning systems off, their names and flags still given by no one. In Asunción, the pretrial detention ordered Saturday stood through its first night. In Kyiv, the president stated the purpose he assigns to Friday night’s barrage: pressure, ahead of Tuesday’s talks in Abu Dhabi. A magnitude 5.7 earthquake struck central Japan at 1:04 a.m. local time and injured more than twenty people, the count still rising through the morning. The Senate count did not move. The desk files the night in that order.

Kraków at 0400: The Three at Home Are Named, and the Country Is in Mourning

The indication the midnight file carried is now an identification. On Sunday morning, Polish police confirmed that the three people found dead at the suspect’s home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski had been identified as his parents and his 21-year-old sister, in the Press Association account filed below. The three were discovered by a drone sent into the flat first, because officers feared explosives might have been planted inside, in the German wire’s morning file; bomb disposal experts later found no explosives in the suspect’s car, though ammunition had been found in it, in the running account filed below. No cause or time of the three deaths at the home has been stated by any authority. The case’s dead therefore stand at nine: six in the Main Market Square — four women and two men, three of them Polish, one a British citizen, two not yet identified, in the police commander’s Saturday-night statement — and three in a block of flats two hours’ drive away. Prosecutors’ spokesman Tomasz Waszczuk has confirmed that the man detained is 24-year-old Michał O., according to Polish media carried in the running account; prosecutors are investigating with the Internal Security Agency, examining ideological and personal motives, and have not established where he obtained his weapons. Polish media, citing unofficial sources, describe a lathe operator who held a sporting firearms permit, had two guns registered in his name, and trained at a shooting club in Starachowice. No charges have been announced; whether and when he can be questioned depends on his condition in hospital, where he remains after several operations, in stable but very critical condition in the last full account.

Sunday in Poland is the first day of the mourning, and the morning’s file is a file of care and ceremony. The two days of national mourning began at midnight under the president’s signed order. Twelve of the injured were in critical or life-threatening condition, Governor Krzysztof Klęczar said, in the German wire’s file. Two of Kraków’s horse-drawn carriage drivers, who work the rank on the square, are among the most seriously injured and are fighting for their lives, Radio Kraków reported Sunday morning; the rank is closed, and hospitals have appealed for blood donors, including for the officer shot three times while stopping the gunman. Five carriage drivers are among the injured in total, in Polish media accounts. A Mass for the victims is set for 4 p.m. local time Sunday at St. Mary’s Basilica, celebrated by Cardinal Grzegorz Ryś; the football association has asked for a minute’s silence before this weekend’s matches; condolences arrived overnight from Czech President Petr Pavel and Prime Minister Andrej Babiš, added to Saturday’s file. Evidence gathering at the scene was expected to continue until at least Sunday, Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said Saturday evening. Separately, police detained a 23-year-old man armed with a knife on Kapelanka Street overnight, after officers fired shots; police have not said whether that incident is connected to Saturday’s attack, and the desk files it as a separate report, unconnected on the record. The interior minister’s reading stands where the day left it — the suspect acted alone and held very radical views, with indications of fascination with far-right ideology still to be investigated — and it remains a reading. No motive has been established by any investigator, and no charge has been announced.

Jerusalem at 0400: A Mandate for Mr. Eisenkot

Israel’s president has made the night’s one new appointment, and it goes to the opposition. President Isaac Herzog informed Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot on Saturday evening of his intention to task him with forming the next government, and invited him to the President’s Residence for the formal ceremony on Sunday at 5 p.m. local time, in the Media Line account and the Reuters account filed below. The decision followed a week of consultations in which factions representing 67 of the Knesset’s 120 members recommended Mr. Eisenkot and 46 recommended Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu; the seven lawmakers of United Torah Judaism recommended neither, in the coalition arithmetic account filed below. The October 27 election left Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc with 53 seats and Mr. Eisenkot’s four-party alliance with 48 — his own Yashar holding 21 — with the Arab-led parties holding 19 between them, and no bloc at the 61 required for a majority. Mr. Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, will have 28 days from the handover to assemble a coalition, with a possible extension of 14. Mr. Netanyahu remains prime minister while the negotiations run. If Mr. Eisenkot succeeds, he takes over from the country’s longest-serving premier; if he fails, the mandate passes to another candidate or back to the Knesset.

The arithmetic that gave him the mandate is not the arithmetic of a government, and the overnight files say so in plain terms. The 67 recommendations include the Arab-led parties whose support Mr. Eisenkot has ruled out as formal coalition partners: one account divides his recommendations as 48 from his own bloc, 7 from Ra’am, and 12 from the Joint List, in the IANS account filed below, while the seat counts in other files give the Joint List 11 and Ra’am 8, for the same total of 19 — the split is printed in the Cocked Hat. Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu sits inside Mr. Eisenkot’s alliance, has said he will oppose a government dependent on Arab-led parties. The path to 61 therefore runs through parties that did not recommend him, including the ultra-Orthodox, or through a form of outside support his own allies resist. Mr. Eisenkot’s first words on the mandate, in the accounts filed below, were: “Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy.” The statement is a claim about intention; the seats are the record. Sunday’s ceremony starts the 28-day clock, and nothing in the night’s file shortens it.

Hormuz at 0400: Two Tankers, a Rescue, and No Names

The Guards’ full statement reached the file overnight, and it is precise about everything except the ships. Two oil tankers violating regulations — one in the eastern part of the Strait of Hormuz and the other within the strait — “caught fire and are currently engulfed in intense flames after striking naval mines while attempting to cross through unauthorised routes,” the Revolutionary Guards said on Sunday, according to IRNA, in the Dhaka file filed below. Both tankers had committed multiple violations, including switching off their navigation and positioning systems, the statement added. The Guards did not specify the name or nationality of either tanker. The same file carries IRNA’s separate report of the Saturday-evening sounds — explosions heard in Qeshm, Sirik, Jask, and Bandar Abbas, their cause unknown — and one new official word inside it: officials confirmed an “impact” in the port city of Jask. What the impact was, and what made it, no official statement in the file says. Reuters’ updated file, filed below, keeps the two halves of the waterway’s night separate, as the desk does: it was not immediately clear whether the tanker incidents were linked to the sounds heard on land. Against the Guards’ mines stands a sentence from the American side carried in the same Dhaka file: Central Command has recently said that all mines have been cleared from the waterway. Both sentences are in the record, attributed, and the desk does not reconcile them.

The night’s one completed act in the waterway is a rescue, and it arrives with a connection asserted around it that its own statement does not make. The United Arab Emirates National Guard said on Sunday that its Coast Guard rescued all 22 crew of a cargo ship that caught fire in the Gulf of Oman, after the crew reported the fire; the men, all Arab nationals, received first aid and were handed to the authorities, all in stable condition, in the maritime account filed below. The National Guard did not name the ship or its flag and did not say what caused the fire. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations had received a report on Saturday of an incident involving a bulk carrier and military forces about 18 nautical miles east of Khor Fakkan, in the UKMTO account filed below, which counts it the sixth vessel incident reported in the corridor this month; the vessel’s crew, damage, and environmental consequences were unknown when the notice was published. Central Command, in the fuller accounts now filed, identified the vessel it disabled late Saturday as the St. Kitts-flagged M/V Huda and said an aircraft fired precision munitions at its stern, in the regional account filed below. Some accounts connect the rescued crew to the disabled ship. The National Guard’s statement does not, and the desk does not: on the record at 0400, the Gulf of Oman holds a disabled ship with a name and no crew report, and a rescued crew of 22 with no ship’s name, and no authority has put the two together.

The diplomacy under the waterway acquired a name overnight: the vice president’s. Vice President JD Vance has spent the past fortnight directly engaged in the indirect negotiations with Iran aimed at a new ceasefire and resumed nuclear talks, Axios reported, in the account filed below: near-daily discussions with Qatar’s prime minister and Pakistan’s army chief, a formal letter a fortnight ago to Mohsen Rezaei of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council proposing resumed direct talks, Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner engaged alongside, a working-level technical meeting discussed and not yet held, and the vice president’s office declining comment. The president remains amenable to letting the effort proceed, the account’s officials say, with American forces ready to strike if he orders it. The report is a report of a backchannel, sourced to two people with knowledge of it; no government has confirmed its terms. It stands beside Saturday’s public record — progress claimed in Washington and Doha, no agreement, no text — as the night’s one new bearing on the talks, and the larger decision on resuming the war in full was again not announced.

Asunción at 0400: The Detention’s First Night

Nothing in the Asunción file moved overnight, and the desk files the stillness with the sequence now complete. The detention ordered Saturday by Judge Humberto Otazú stood through its first night: former President Santiago Peña held before trial at a military facility — the headquarters of the Presidential Escort Regiment, in the local accounts — and former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo held in a detention center, on the charges the evening filed, breach of trust and administration for personal gain against both men and producing false public documents against Mr. Carvallo besides. The fuller wire account filed below completes the custody sequence the day’s editions carried in pieces: house arrest on Friday, a move to the military facility Friday night for security reasons as protests gathered outside his home, and Saturday’s pretrial order as a separate court decision following the formal charges. Mr. Peña’s plea stands at not guilty, through his attorney, Ricardo Preda; each of his two charges could carry up to ten years, the prosecutor said. President Pedro Alliana governs into his second full day, and the deposit-guarantee ledger stands at $160 million paid to nearly 1.2 million savers. Protests over the Ueno collapse continue in the accounts. Sunday in Asunción is a day without a scheduled court item in any file the desk took in; the case’s next facts will be procedural — the asset-freeze requests and the six months prosecutors asked to formulate the final case — and none arrived in the night.

Kyiv at 0400: Pressure, Stated as Pressure

Ukraine’s president has put his reading of Friday night’s barrage on the record, and the overnight files carry it whole. Russia is ramping up its attacks to put pressure on Ukraine and its partners at the trilateral talks, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday, in the Arab News account filed below: “By intensifying its attacks on Ukraine and our infrastructure at this very moment, Russia is trying to additionally lay the groundwork for putting pressure on Ukraine’s position and that of its partners.” The barrage itself stands as the evening and midnight editions filed it — 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones in the president’s count, four missiles intercepted, nine people wounded including a child in the Associated Press account filed below — with the damage ledger filled in overnight: the energy ministry’s statement that a massive attack on energy facilities plunged five regions into darkness, consumers in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Kyiv, Zhytomyr, and Kharkiv left without power and transmission in the capital significantly hampered, as temperatures drop toward winter. The president’s account adds that missiles among the 36 were KN-23s manufactured and supplied by North Korea, and that the interception figure reflects a shortage of Patriot interceptors. The reading — pressure — is the president’s; the ministry’s ledger is the file’s. Russia’s defence ministry’s own overnight figures run the other way: 411 Ukrainian drones shot down over ten Russian regions, and one person killed in Russia’s Belgorod region when a Ukrainian drone hit a private home in Grayvoron, in the Guardian’s war briefing filed below. The talks open in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, November 10 and 11 — the fourth American-brokered round, the last in Geneva in February — with both delegations named, as the midnight edition filed them. No agenda, draft, or text has been published by any side.

The Count at 0400: A Sunday Without Figures

Neither Senate race was called in the night, and no new figure was published for either. The overnight accounts restate the standing figures without changing them: in Mississippi, the Democrat, Scott Colom, leads the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, by 2,574 votes in the wire’s Friday tally — 467,930 to 465,356, about 49.1 percent to 48.8 with the independent just over 2 percent — in the Saturday update and the two-races account filed below; in Alaska, the Democrat, Mary Peltola, leads the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, by 637 first-choice votes at 48.2 to 47.9, with roughly 74 percent of the expected vote counted. Sunday is a counting day in neither state’s published procedure. The count speaks next on Tuesday, November 10, three times over: Alaska’s next update is scheduled that day and is expected to carry almost all the early votes and a large batch of absentee ballots; Mississippi’s mail ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive by that day, and its boards of commissioners have until that day to complete the counting of provisional ballots. Counties certify by November 13; Alaska’s absentee ballots arrive through November 18, when the ranked-choice tabulation is set if no candidate reaches 50 percent. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide, and Colorado’s 4th District stands uncalled with them, the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, ahead by 3,172 votes in Friday’s figures. The House tallies in the Sunday accounts do not agree with each other — one Sunday explainer carries 248 seats called for the Democrats and 37 races uncalled, against the wire-based tallies of Saturday — and the disagreement is printed in the Cocked Hat.

Shizuoka at 0400: A 5.7 in the Night, the Count of the Hurt Still Rising

Central Japan supplied the night’s one act of nature, at 1:04 a.m. local time. An earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 5.7 struck western Shizuoka Prefecture at a depth of about 40 kilometres, registering upper 5 on the Japanese seismic intensity scale in Chita, Aichi Prefecture — the strongest shaking observed in Aichi since March 1997, and upper 5 in western Shizuoka for the first time in 107 years, in the Kyodo account and the morning account filed below. The American survey measured the same quake at 5.5; the two magnitudes are printed in the Cocked Hat. No tsunami warning was issued. The early accounts counted three injured — a woman in her 50s taken to hospital with a fractured ankle in Tokoname, and a man in his 40s and a woman in her 80s who fell and struck their heads in Toyota, both conscious, in the first full account filed below — and the morning’s counts rose past twenty injured across Aichi and Shizuoka, with the tallies still differing by source at 0400. No abnormalities were detected at the Hamaoka nuclear power plant, its operator said, and the meteorological agency assessed the possibility that the quake was linked to a Nankai Trough megaquake as low, while advising residents in the strongly shaken areas to stay alert for about a week for further tremors up to upper 5, particularly in the next two to three days. Tokaido Shinkansen trains ran at reduced speed between Shizuoka and Gifu-Hashima and had resumed normal speed before noon local time; the central government set up a liaison office. Sunday in the region is an assessment day; the injury count is the figure still moving.

Sunday Opens: Mourning, Lights, a Ceremony, and a Monday

The day the night hands over is an observance day on three calendars at once. In Poland it is the first of two days of national mourning, with Kraków’s own mourning running through November 11 and the victims’ Mass at St. Mary’s at 4 p.m. In India it is the main day of Diwali, the festival of lights, whose five days run from Dhanteras on November 6 to Bhai Dooj on November 11, with Lakshmi Puja at dusk. In Jerusalem at 5 p.m. local time, the presidency formally hands Mr. Eisenkot his mandate and starts his 28 days. The markets are closed; Monday’s open will be the first to price a weekend that put two tankers on fire in the world’s oil strait, and Monday is also the day Stephen Miller takes office as chief of staff in Washington, the appointment the evening edition filed, and the first working day of the new Congress’s majority in the chamber the voters have already decided. Everything the week left open with a date on it carries Tuesday’s date: the Abu Dhabi talks open, the American inflation report is due, Mississippi’s mail deadline and Alaska’s next count fall, and the president’s larger Iran decision, promised Thursday and not announced in four editions since, has no date at all. The log proceeds to Sunday.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On Kraków’s suspect, the police accounts give his age as 24 and the updated international files give 25; the prosecutors’ spokesman’s confirmation, as carried in Polish media, gives 24 and a name, Michał O. On the wounded, the counts run 15 injured, 16 in hospital including the two officers and the suspect himself, and 12 in critical or life-threatening condition within them — three true sentences counting three different sets. On the distance from Kraków to the house in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, the files give 93 miles, about 120 miles, and just under 200 kilometres. On the three at the house, the overnight police caution — most likely his parents and sister, formal confirmation when the scene work finishes — stands in the running account beside the Sunday-morning police confirmation, in the Press Association account, that the three have been identified as his parents and his 21-year-old sister; the desk prints the confirmation as the later and fuller bearing, and the caution as the record of how it arrived. On Japan’s quake, the meteorological agency gives magnitude 5.7 and the American survey 5.5, and the injured run 3 in the first full account, 15 in a morning tally, and over 20, 22, and 24 in the later ones, by prefecture and by hour. On Israel’s Arab-led parties, the files agree on 19 seats and divide them 11 and 8 and also 12 and 7, between the Joint List and Ra’am. On the House, one Sunday tally counts 248 Democratic seats called and 37 races open, where Saturday’s wire-based accounts counted more called and fewer open; the Senate figures, by contrast, are single-valued in every account: 2,574 and 637, uncalled. On Hormuz’s tankers, the statements now agree on two, and agree on nothing else that would let a reader find them: no name, no flag, no crew, no confirmation independent of the Guards — beside an American statement, in the same files, that all mines in the waterway have been cleared. Against the triangle, the night’s single-valued facts are these: the three at the Kraków house are identified as the suspect’s parents and sister, and Poland’s mourning has begun; Mr. Eisenkot has been chosen to try first at a government, with the ceremony Sunday and 28 days to run; 22 crew are rescued and stable in the Gulf of Oman, from a ship no authority has named; the Guards say two tankers are burning on mines, and no side has named them; Mr. Peña spent the night in pretrial detention; the Abu Dhabi delegations stand named for Tuesday; no Senate race was called; and central Japan was shaken at upper 5 for the first time in 107 years, with more than twenty hurt and the count still rising. The log proceeds to Sunday.

### Three More Dead in Kraków, a Judge Jails Peña, and Tankers Burn in Hormuz

Filed as: Edition No. 18 — The Midnight Watch · 2026-11-08T00:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-08-midnight-watch.html

The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Three More Dead in Kraków, a Judge Jails Peña, and Tankers Burn in Hormuz

 The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: Saturday settled the detention question in Asunción, where a judge ordered the removed president and the former central bank chief held before trial, and it settled Berkshire Hathaway’s quarter on paper. It deepened the Kraków case, where police searching the suspect’s home found three more bodies, and it closed with explosions across Iran’s Hormuz coast, two tankers reported on fire, and an American disabling of a vessel in the Gulf of Oman—while the larger Iran decision, the Senate count, and the Abu Dhabi talks all stayed open, waiting on Tuesday.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Sunday, November 8, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 16, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Saturday, and in the day’s earlier editions, Nos. 14 and 15. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Saturday Settled, What It Left Open

Saturday settled a detention, a quarter’s accounts, and nothing else it was asked to settle. In Asunción, Judge Humberto Otazú ordered former President Santiago Peña held in pretrial detention at a military facility and former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo held in a detention center, a ruling the Evening Watch left pending at 1800; Mr. Peña’s attorney said he is pleading not guilty. In Kraków, the day’s count of the dead grew by three without a shot in the square: police searching the suspect’s home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski found two women and a man dead, and the prime minister told a late briefing there are strong indications the three are members of the suspect’s immediate family. The six dead in the Main Market Square stand as filed at evening—four women and two men, one of them a British citizen—with sixteen wounded in the police commander’s count, and national mourning begins today, Sunday, November 8, running through Monday, with the city’s mourning through November 11. In the Strait of Hormuz, Saturday evening brought explosions heard on Qeshm Island and at Jask, Sirik, and Bandar Abbas, a report from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy that two oil tankers hit mines on an unauthorized route and caught fire, and an American statement that Central Command late Saturday disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship that ignored warnings and tried to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port. No American statement by midnight claimed the explosions, and no Iranian statement by midnight explained them as a strike. The larger Iran decision promised Thursday was not announced. The count did not move: Mississippi and Alaska stand uncalled for a fourth day, Colorado’s 4th stands uncalled with it, and the talks in Abu Dhabi open Tuesday, November 10, with both delegations now named. Sunday is Diwali’s main day in India, and Poland’s mourning. The desk files the day in that order.

Kraków at Midnight: Three More Bodies, at the Suspect’s Home

The evening’s new fact in Kraków was found 120 miles from the square. CNN’s updated file, filed below, reports that police discovered the bodies of three people—two women and a man—during a search of the suspect’s home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 120 miles north of Kraków, and found many weapons and ammunition in his vehicle. Prime Minister Donald Tusk told the late Saturday crisis meeting in Kraków that there were “strong indications” the three are members of the suspect’s immediate family. That indication is filed as an indication; no identification of the three has been published, and no cause or time of their deaths has been stated by any authority in the files taken in by midnight. The square attack itself stands as the evening filed it: reports began at about 3 p.m. local time, the suspect drove into the Main Market Square firing at random, six people were killed, and police shot and arrested him. The wounded figures and the suspect’s age do not agree across the late files, and the desk prints the disagreement in the cocked hat below.

What Saturday night added on the record is care for the wounded and a country entering mourning. The same CNN file reports the suspect underwent multiple surgeries and is in stable but very critical condition; that the two wounded police officers both underwent surgery and are in stable condition, one shot once and the other three times; that the justice minister said one officer has a non-functioning lung and urgently requires AB+ blood; and that the injured include five foreign nationals, from Austria, Germany, Portugal, Russia, and Britain, in an Interior Ministry spokesperson’s account. The British account records the police commander’s statement that three Polish persons, one citizen of Great Britain, and two persons not yet identified make up the six dead, and the foreign secretary’s statement mourning the British national and the other victims. The interior minister’s reading stands where the evening left it: everything points to the shooter having been influenced by far-right ideology, a matter to be investigated. No charge had been announced by midnight, and no motive has been established. Poland’s president will declare national mourning for November 8 and 9; Kraków’s mayor has declared mourning in the city until November 11. Sunday therefore opens in Poland as a day of mourning over nine dead in one case—six in a public square, three in a private house—with the connection between the two sets of deaths stated by the prime minister as a strong indication and by no investigator yet as a finding.

Asunción at Midnight: The Judge Rules, Both Men Held

The question the Evening Watch left at the courthouse door was answered Saturday night. Reuters’ late Asunción file, filed below, reports that Judge Humberto Otazú ordered former President Santiago Peña held in pretrial detention at a military facility, saying detention was necessary to ensure he remained in the country while the case proceeded, and ordered former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo to pretrial detention in a holding center. The charges stand as filed at evening: breach of trust and administration for personal gain against Mr. Peña, and those charges plus producing false public documents against Mr. Carvallo. Prosecutors allege Mr. Peña used his position to influence agencies and state entities to keep large amounts of public money deposited at Ueno despite his financial ties to the lender; he was a shareholder in Ueno’s holding company until March 2025. His attorney, Ricardo Preda, told journalists Mr. Peña is pleading not guilty and said, “We will submit to the investigation and I am sure that when this investigation is over the result will be the dismissal.” Mr. Peña has denied wrongdoing and said the bank’s problems were a regulatory matter. Mr. Carvallo did not respond to a request for comment in the Reuters file. The two charges against Mr. Peña could carry up to ten years in prison each, the prosecutor said.

The rest of the Asunción file stands settled where the day left it, and the desk keeps the two ledgers separate. The central bank’s Saturday figure stands: the equivalent of $160 million paid out to nearly 1.2 million savers under the deposit guarantee scheme, against a lender that served about three million customers. President Pedro Alliana, sworn in Friday to complete Mr. Peña’s term through August 2028, governs; protests over the Ueno case continue in the accounts filed below, with some sectors calling for early elections. What changed at midnight is narrow and complete: detention, asked at midday and charged at evening, is now ordered. The allegations remain allegations, the plea is not guilty, and the case proceeds with both men in custody—the first former president in this file to pass from removal to a cell in two days, on the record as filed.

Hormuz at Midnight: Explosions on the Coast, Tankers on Fire, a Vessel Disabled

Saturday evening produced three separate reports from one waterway, and the desk files them as three reports, not one event. First, the explosions. Reuters’ Cairo file reports explosions heard Saturday evening in several areas in southern Iran, including on Qeshm Island; that state television suggested the explosions might be linked to Iranian military activities in the waterway; that officials have not confirmed any missile strikes; and that Tasnim, citing a source, said the explosions on Qeshm were not related to missile strikes—while Tasnim also said earlier Saturday that two missiles struck Qeshm Island, with no official information on damage. A second account widens the list of places to Qeshm, Jask, Sirik, and Bandar Abbas, and carries a report of casualties at Jask with no number given, a claim that stands unconfirmed in every other file. Second, the tankers. The Revolutionary Guards Navy said early Sunday, in the Reuters file, that two oil tankers were on fire after hitting mines as they attempted to pass through an “unauthorized route” in the strait; the Iranian military’s late Saturday account, in the Associated Press file filed below, says two tankers hit mines and caught fire and does not identify their flags or destinations. One tanker or two, and at which exit of the strait, are stated differently across the day’s Iranian statements collected in the files below; the desk prints both tellings in the cocked hat. Third, the vessel. Central Command said late Saturday it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship after it ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port, in the Associated Press file—a confirmed American act, stated by the command itself, in the Gulf of Oman. The same file notes the disclosure follows at least two instances in which the command did not announce strikes it had taken in the region. No file taken in by midnight connects the explosions, the mines, and the disabled ship into one operation, and the desk does not connect them.

The day’s other Iran facts are announcements, and they point in opposite directions, as announcements can. In Tehran, the Revolutionary Guards’ spokesman said the self-imposed limit of 2,000 kilometres on ballistic missile ranges “has been lifted for us,” following the supreme leader’s order that threats be answered without geographical limits, in the wire account and the fuller account filed below; both carry the spokesman’s own caution that capability must be demonstrated in practice, and no file shows a missile demonstrated beyond the old limit. In Tampa, Central Command announced Task Force Iron Gate, about twenty military and civilian personnel directed by Admiral Brad Cooper to coordinate with other agencies against the movement of advanced weapons, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea, in the account filed below; the command said its naval blockade has prevented more than $25 billion in Iranian crude exports, a figure that is the command’s own estimate. In Ankara, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told President Trump by telephone that tensions between the United States and Iran should be resolved through diplomacy and that Ankara would continue its peace efforts, and that contacts with Kyiv and Moscow should be intensified, in the readout account filed below; the Turkish readout announced no agreement and no new mediation role. The president’s Friday words stand as the latest American position on the talks—progress claimed, no details given—beside Qatar’s statement that significant progress has been made. The larger decision on resuming the war in full was not announced on Saturday. At midnight the Hormuz file therefore reads: a range limit lifted in words, a task force stood up on paper, a ship disabled at sea, tankers reported burning, explosions unexplained, and diplomacy urged by telephone. Only two of those six items are acts at sea, and both are stated by the side that performed or reported them, without independent confirmation in the files.

Kyiv and Abu Dhabi at Midnight: The Delegations Named, the Damage Counted Three Ways

The talks acquired their full cast on Saturday, and the war acquired a fresh damage ledger the same day. The trilateral talks open in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, November 10 and 11, the first since February. Russia’s delegation will be led by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky and will include Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov, and General Staff officer Yuri Zhigarlovsky, in the Reuters account filed below. Ukraine’s team will be led by Rustem Umerov, with Presidential Office chief Kyrylo Budanov also participating, and the United States is expected to be represented by Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, in the second account filed below. The strikes of the night between Friday and Saturday stand as the evening filed them, with the figures unreconciled: President Zelenskyy’s account gives 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones over Kyiv and twelve other regions, four missiles intercepted, and nine people wounded including a child; the wire’s account gives at least five injured in Kyiv; a city account gives two. Russia’s defence ministry confirmed it targeted the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro, saying it facilitated the transport of weaponry and military equipment. In Kyiv, Mr. Zelenskyy’s Saturday address also carried the corruption file forward: he called the alleged crimes in Operation Carthage “frankly shameful, absolutely unacceptable,” said dismissals at the security service have occurred and more personnel decisions will follow, and proposed legislation requiring all security-service employees to publicly declare their assets, in the accounts filed with the Evening Watch. No agreement, draft, or agenda for Abu Dhabi has been published by any side. Tuesday carries the talks’ opening beside the American inflation report and the count’s next deadlines, and nothing in Saturday’s file shortens that list.

The Count at Midnight: A Fourth Day Without a Call

Neither Senate race was called on Saturday, and the published figures for the two races did not move. In Mississippi, the Democrat, Scott Colom, leads the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, by some 2,500 votes in the wire’s tally, at about 49.1 percent to 48.8 percent with the independent candidate just over 2 percent, in the Saturday account and the count update filed below. The estimates of what remains run where they ran: roughly 30,000 ballots possibly outstanding in the wire’s Friday estimate, roughly 20,000 in the Republican estimate carried Saturday, about 3,600 mail ballots in the secretary of state’s Wednesday statement, and an unknown number of affidavit ballots. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day arrive through Tuesday, November 10, voters may resolve ballot problems through the same date, and counties certify by November 13. In Alaska, the Democrat, Mary Peltola, leads the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, by 637 first-choice votes, at 48.2 percent to 47.9 percent with roughly three-quarters of the expected vote reported, unchanged since Wednesday; absentee ballots arrive through November 18, when the ranked-choice tabulation is set, no candidate standing above 50 percent. The legal fronts stand as filed: the Justice Department’s suit over the second candidate named Daniel Sullivan dismissed before the voting, with an appeal pledged, and the Peltola campaign’s Friday records suit over rejected absentee ballots. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide. In the House, Colorado’s 3rd stands called for Representative Jeff Hurd, and Colorado’s 4th stands uncalled, the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, ahead of Representative Lauren Boebert by 3,172 votes at 6 p.m. Friday in the district account filed below—a margin outside the automatic-recount line of about 923 votes, with the cure deadline on November 12—while the Boebert campaign says it is investigating what it calls unusual voting patterns and expects a recount. The count speaks next on Tuesday.

The Week, Settled on Paper: Berkshire’s Quarter

The one scheduled report of Saturday arrived in the morning and closed the market week’s accounts. Berkshire Hathaway’s third quarter, in the accounts filed below: operating earnings of $12.705 billion, down 5.8 percent from $13.485 billion a year earlier; net earnings of $22.112 billion, down 28 percent; insurance underwriting profit down 43 percent; share repurchases of $9.6 billion in the quarter, more than double the second quarter’s $4.5 billion and about $14.4 billion for the year; and cash and Treasury bills at a record $377.435 billion at the end of September, up from $365.514 billion at the end of June. The exchanges were closed, and the week stands as filed at midday: the S&P 500 down 2.7 percent, Brent crude at $98.32, down 13.3 percent on the week. Monday’s open waits on the Hormuz file, as Friday’s close waited on it. Sunday carries no scheduled market item. It carries Poland’s national mourning, beginning today, and in India the main day of Diwali, the festival of lights, whose five days run from Dhanteras on November 6 to Bhai Dooj on November 11, with Lakshmi Puja at dusk today, in the festival account filed below. The desk records both observances in one line each, as the log records what the day is, beside what the day did.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. On Kraków’s suspect, the police accounts give his age as 24 and the updated international file gives 25; on the wounded, the afternoon’s official count is fifteen, the police commander’s evening count is sixteen taken to hospital, and one later account counts the wounded suspect among the sixteen. On Hormuz’s tankers, the day’s Iranian statements collected in the files speak of one tanker ablaze at the eastern exit in one telling and two tankers on fire after hitting mines in two others; the desk prints the statements as statements, attributed, and notes that no name, flag, or independent confirmation stands in any of them. On Mississippi’s outstanding ballots, Saturday’s estimates run from about 3,600 mail ballots, in the secretary of state’s figure, to roughly 20,000 in the Republican estimate and roughly 30,000 in the wire’s; the lead is some 2,500 votes in every Saturday account. On Kyiv’s injured, the figures remain two, five, and nine, from a city account, the wire, and the president. Against the triangle, the midnight facts that are single-valued are these: three bodies were found at the Kraków suspect’s home, and six people are dead in the square, with mourning beginning today; Peña and Carvallo are ordered held before trial, on charges both files state the same way, and Mr. Peña pleads not guilty through his attorney; Central Command disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship in the Gulf of Oman, by its own statement, and announced a twenty-person task force in Tampa; explosions were heard across Iran’s Hormuz coast and their cause is confirmed by no authority; the missile-range limit is lifted in words, with no missile shown beyond it; both Abu Dhabi delegations are named and the talks open Tuesday; no Senate race was called; and Berkshire’s quarter is on paper at $12.705 billion in operating earnings and $377.435 billion in cash. Saturday settled a detention, a quarter, and a week. It left open a war at sea, a count in two states, a motive in Kraków, and a negotiation in Abu Dhabi. The log turns to Sunday.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-six items.

 

 SubjectiveCNN — after the Kraków rampage, three more bodies found at the suspect’s homeAt least six people killed and sixteen wounded when a gunman opened fire from his car in Kraków on Saturday, officials said, adding that three more people were found dead at his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 120 miles north; the suspect, a 25-year-old Polish citizen, was shot and injured by police, underwent multiple surgeries, and is in stable but very critical condition; the two wounded officers are in stable condition after surgery; the justice minister said one officer has a non-functioning lung and urgently requires AB+ blood; the injured include five foreign nationals from Austria, Germany, Portugal, Russia, and Britain; and Prime Minister Tusk told a late briefing there were strong indications the three bodies are members of the suspect’s immediate family.

 SubjectiveThe Oldham Times — investigations continue as a Briton is among six killed in PolandInvestigations are ongoing after a British citizen was among the six people killed in Kraków; the suspected gunman, a 25-year-old Polish national believed to have been inspired by far-right ideologies, remains in hospital after being shot by police; the police commander said sixteen people were injured including two police officers and the perpetrator himself, eleven of them Polish citizens and five foreign; the dead are three Polish persons, one citizen of Great Britain, and two persons not yet identified; the prime minister said another three bodies were found at the gunman’s home about 93 miles from Kraków; and the foreign secretary said the United Kingdom deeply mourns the British national and the other victims.

 SubjectiveReuters, via EuropeSays — Poland in shock as six dead after the mass shooting in KrakowKrakow, November 7: a gunman likely influenced by far-right ideology killed six people shooting randomly from a car in the main square before police shot and arrested him; the interior minister said five foreigners were among the sixteen wounded taken to hospital and four of the dead had been identified, one a foreigner; a Portuguese woman is among the injured; the assailant used an AR-15 rifle and held a firearms licence, a police spokesperson said, and police gave his age as 24; and the president will declare national mourning on November 8 and 9.

 SubjectivePeople — at least 6 dead, 15 injured after a man drove into the market square and opened fireNovember 7: a man drove into Kraków’s Main Market Square at about 3 p.m. local time and fired at random from his car, killing at least six and injuring fifteen, including two police officers, one shot three times and in very critical condition; the toll was first reported as five dead and later confirmed at six; the dead are four women and two men, not yet publicly identified; police denied reports that an officer had died or that another perpetrator was being sought; the gunman was shot by officers, detained, and taken to hospital; and the prime minister offered condolences and appealed to politicians not to exploit the tragedy.

 SubjectiveFish4News — six killed and 16 injured in the Kraków shootingSix people killed and sixteen injured after a gunman opened fire from a car in Kraków’s historic centre on Saturday, November 7; police shot and detained the suspect, who authorities say acted alone; an earlier version of the account is corrected to record that a British citizen was among the six killed and five of the wounded were foreign nationals, including a Portuguese woman; the number injured was initially given as fifteen and later reported as sixteen, with some reporting counting the wounded suspect among those hurt; reports give the suspect’s age as 24 in police accounts and 25 in later international reports; and Kraków’s mayor declared city mourning from Sunday, November 8 through Wednesday, November 11, with the president announcing national mourning for November 8 and 9.
